core_themes.name: Lower NICs for the self-employed
core_themes.claim: Self-employed people pay lower NICs than employees (9% vs 12% Class 4/Class 1, plus no employer NICs), so the same earnings generate materially less tax and NICs depending on employment status.

core_themes.name: Fiscal cost and growing self-employment
core_themes.claim: The foregone NICs cost the public finances an estimated £5.1 billion in 2016-17, and with self-employment rising as a share of the workforce and the planned Class 2 abolition widening the gap, this poses significant fiscal challenges.

core_themes.name: Narrowed benefit access gap
core_themes.claim: The historical justification for lower self-employed contributions, less state support, has weakened because the new State Pension gives the self-employed the same entitlement as employees, leaving only minor differences in parental benefits and contribution-based JSA.

diagnosis.note: Diagnosis sentences are interleaved with descriptive tax-system detail and worked examples; the core argument is the gap in contributions, its fiscal cost and the erosion of the rationale for it.

core_themes.name: Class 2 abolition and Class 4 increase
core_themes.claim: Class 2 NICs will be abolished and the Class 4 rate raised from 9% to 10% in 2018 and 11% in 2019, which simplifies the system for the self-employed, makes it more progressive and narrows the gap with employee NICs.

core_themes.name: Parity with employees through the new State Pension
core_themes.claim: The Class 4 increase is justified because the self-employed now have the same State Pension as employees, worth up to £1,800 a year more, so the lower contribution rate is no longer warranted.

core_themes.name: Revenue and distributional impact
core_themes.claim: The reforms raise less revenue at first but a net £215 million a year by 2019-20, and protect low-profit earners because only those with profits above £16,250 pay more, with worked examples showing most gain overall once personal allowance rises are included.

proposal.note: The document does not examine alternative options to this package, and some of the proposal-labelled text is worked examples and budget table rows.

implementation.note: Only one sentence is labelled implementation (Class 4 replacing Class 2 as the basis for benefit entitlement from April 2018), which is too thin to support a core theme.
